City needs to fix hiring procedure at Fire Dept.
Editor:
We seek your assistance in
making sure that Piedmont Fire-
fighters are accorded salaries and
health benefits in keeping with
the fact that they are our Pied-
mont citizens’ extended family
in terms of their dedication to our
health and safety.
We moved to Piedmont in
1993 and raised our two chil-
dren here. We have experienced
the intelligence, caring and deci-
sion-making of our Piedmont
Firefighters. Had we not person-
ally benefited from the firefight-
ers’ kindness and skill, we would
still feel tremendous gratitude to
them for being here just in case.
We were very distressed to
read the article in the Septem-
ber 23 Piedmont Post indicating
that negotiations between the
firefighters and the city are at
a standstill. We carefully read
the firefighters’ concerns about
the necessity of 1) having pay
increases to encourage longevity,
and 2) having retirement benefits
to cover firefighters’ medical care
for the period between retirement
and Social Security eligibility.
We share the firefighters’ under-
lying concern about inadequate
staffing which requires excessive
overtime to keep us safe.
As residents and taxpayers, we
support the firefighters’ demands.
Piedmont prides itself on being a
city that is at the forefront of good
decision-making. Piedmont needs
to step up to support the firefight-
ers and to inform its citizens what
efforts and finances are required
to do so. We rely on Piedmont
Firefighters for our lives and the
lives of our children. Is there
anything more important? The
firefighters’ knowledge, skills,
courage and work ethic should
be celebrated and honored by
accepting their demands.
We are both retired attorneys;
Joe represented injured workers
and clients denied social security
disability; I practiced civil rights
law. As residents of Piedmont, we
find the city’s response puzzling
and extraordinarily short-sighted
(using overtime instead of prop-
erly hiring, making the very hir-
ing process discouraging by not
providing the enticement of raises
after certain years of service are
reached, by not meeting the basic
human need of health insurance
until Social Security eligibility is
reached).
We look forward to hearing
from you.
–Susan Goldsmith and
Joseph Waxman

Reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta
Having served eight years on the Piedmont City Council, includ-
ing two years as mayor, I understand deeply that the true measure of
public service is not the popularity of every individual decision; it is
whether the institution is stronger, more accountable, and better pre-
pared for the future when one’s service concludes. That is why I am
again supporting Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College
When I endorsed Cindi in 2022, I noted her educational and accred-
itation experience, devotion to the common good, attention to detail,
intellect and vision. I also recognized her willingness to challenge
entrenched interests in pursuit of sound fiscal management. When
she ran for the Board in 2018, Peralta faced serious financial instabil-
ity, accreditation concerns, leadership turnover, board conflict, board
micromanagement of chancellors and possible state-takeover of the
district. Cindi Reiss has fulfilled those promises.
Today, Peralta is financially and institutionally stronger. Its four
colleges are fully accredited. Stable executive leadership, stronger
financial practices, greater transparency, and more disciplined long-
range planning have replaced years of instability. Recent credit ratings
reflect increased confidence in the District’s governance and financial
direction, while a 2025 bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers
These gains did not happen by accident. Cindi helped foster a Board
culture focused on its proper responsibilities: setting policy, safe-
guarding public resources, requiring accountability, and supporting
strong professional leadership without micromanaging it. She has also
demonstrated the courage to make difficult decisions when the dis-
But recovery is not completion. Peralta must now carry its Trans-
formation Plan from vision into implementation. That means reducing
fragmentation, coordinating programs and services, strengthening path-
ways for students, and building a fiscal structure capable of sustaining
the colleges well beyond the tenure of any trustee or administrator.
As Piedmont residents, we have a direct stake in Peralta’s future, in
its strength and success. Whether it’s through our many Piedmont high
school students that have participated in dual enrollment with Peralta
by taking Calculus III: Partial Differentiation, Discrete Mathematics,
Linear Algebra or business management classes; adults that have taken
art and language classes, or through the thousands of students that Peral-
ta’s colleges serve in Alameda County, Piedmont benefits from a strong
Peralta Community College system. When Peralta helps students earn
degrees, certificates or transfer to universities, and build economically
secure lives, the benefits extend well beyond its campuses.
A strong Peralta means a stronger regional workforce, greater eco-
nomic mobility, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, and a
healthier and more stable East Bay. Our support of Peralta’s colleges
is an investment in the regional institutions and quality of life on
I urge my fellow Piedmonters to reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta
Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3.

LETTERS - MAIN
Yes on Measure GG
Editor,
We are writing to Piedmont
voters to urge a YES vote on Mea-
sure GG. Our families planted
roots in Piedmont more than 100
years ago. We have made our
home here because Piedmont
offers a unique combination of
small-town ambiance with strong
public safety, outstanding public
schools and excellent quality of
life amenities such as beautiful
parks, strong recreation programs
and lovely public spaces.
We believe the financial
experts who are telling us we
soon will have a shortfall in rev-
enues to pay for existing city ser-
vices, facilities and infrastruc-
ture. The cuts that will come if
that happens, most likely starting
with “quality of life” expenses,
threaten the things we hold most
dear about Piedmont.
We believe the small increase
in the real estate transfer tax pro-
posed by Measure GG is the most
painless method of dealing with
the threat. It is only imposed at
a time when property is being
sold—a time when funds are
most likely to be available to
make a payment. Your YES vote
on Measure GG will help pre-
serve the Piedmont that has kept
our families here for so long.
–Fran Bishopric Wolfe and
Cameron Wolfe, Jr.
Support Measure GG:
Support our community
Editor,
My family moved to Pied-
mont for the schools AND for
the public safety. Having a local
police and fire department won’t
protect everyone from all crimes
and accidents, but knowing that
our professional first responders
have the ability to respond in 5
minutes or less is very reassuring.
These services are paid for by
tax dollars which are allocated
annually by our elected leaders,
supported by volunteer financial
experts, and professional city
staff. The entire process is public
and the proposed and approved
budgets are posted on the City’s
web site at https://piedmont.
ca.gov. The budget reflects our
community’s priorities of fiscal
responsibility and public safety.
This is reflected in the fact that
the vast majority of operating
expenditures go to the police, fire,
and public works departments.
When people ask me what
Measure GG will support, I tell
them it will support what our
community values. It will support
all the things that make Piedmont
a safe place to live and raise our
families. Please join me in voting
Yes on Measure GG.
–Kim Hunter
Retired Alameda County
Senior Deputy District Attorney
Keep Piedmont
moving forward with
Measure GG
Dear Editor,
When I was young, Piedmont
Recreation Department pro-
grams were instrumental in my
development and helped form
the person I am today. When I
was fortunate enough to serve as
Piedmont’s Recreation Director
and later as City Administrator,
I gained insight into the ongoing
cost of the many services pro-
vided by the City of Piedmont to
the community. From streets to
parks, sidewalks to police cars,
fire apparatus to building mainte-
nance, the costs to provide essen-
tial services to Piedmont have
continued to rise.
Piedmont is one of a small
number of California cities
whose revenues are primarily
property based. This funding
structure severely limits options
for increased revenues needed to
keep Piedmont from falling fur-
ther behind. Measure GG is a rea-
sonable way to provide additional
and ongoing funds to support city
services, while not placing an
ongoing burden on property own-
ers. If approved, Measure GG
will bring Piedmont’s transfer tax
more in line with our surrounding
communities and provide approx-
imately $1.5 million in additional
revenue to support essential ser-
vices and city infrastructure.
Piedmonters understand the
value of ongoing investment,
especially in community services
and assets. Supporting Measure
GG is a way to keep up and keep
Piedmont moving forward for
years to come.
Sincerely,
Sara Lillevand

District Board.
When I endorsed Cindi in 2022, I noted her educational and accred-
itation experience, devotion to the common good, attention to detail,
intellect and vision. I also recognized her willingness to challenge
entrenched interests in pursuit of sound fiscal management. When
she ran for the Board in 2018, Peralta faced serious financial instabil-
ity, accreditation concerns, leadership turnover, board conflict, board
micromanagement of chancellors and possible state-takeover of the
district. Cindi Reiss has fulfilled those promises.
Today, Peralta is financially and institutionally stronger. Its four
colleges are fully accredited. Stable executive leadership, stronger
financial practices, greater transparency, and more disciplined long-
range planning have replaced years of instability. Recent credit ratings
reflect increased confidence in the District’s governance and financial
direction, while a 2025 bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers
$13.7 million.
These gains did not happen by accident. Cindi helped foster a Board
culture focused on its proper responsibilities: setting policy, safe-
guarding public resources, requiring accountability, and supporting
strong professional leadership without micromanaging it. She has also
demonstrated the courage to make difficult decisions when the dis-
trict’s long-term interests required them.
But recovery is not completion. Peralta must now carry its Trans-
formation Plan from vision into implementation. That means reducing
fragmentation, coordinating programs and services, strengthening path-
ways for students, and building a fiscal structure capable of sustaining
the colleges well beyond the tenure of any trustee or administrator.
As Piedmont residents, we have a direct stake in Peralta’s future, in
its strength and success. Whether it’s through our many Piedmont high
school students that have participated in dual enrollment with Peralta
by taking Calculus III: Partial Differentiation, Discrete Mathematics,
Linear Algebra or business management classes; adults that have taken
art and language classes, or through the thousands of students that Peral-
ta’s colleges serve in Alameda County, Piedmont benefits from a strong
Peralta Community College system. When Peralta helps students earn
degrees, certificates or transfer to universities, and build economically
secure lives, the benefits extend well beyond its campuses.
A strong Peralta means a stronger regional workforce, greater eco-
nomic mobility, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, and a
healthier and more stable East Bay. Our support of Peralta’s colleges
is an investment in the regional institutions and quality of life on
which Piedmont itself depends.
I urge my fellow Piedmonters to reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta
Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3.
Best,
Teddy Gray King

Community invited to Mayor Andersen’s
State of the City address on Oct. 15
Mayor Betsy Smegal Ander-
sen will deliver Piedmont’s
2026 State of the City address
on Thursday, October 15, at
5:30 p.m. in Community Hall.
The evening is a chance to come
together as a community to cele-
brate Piedmont, reflect on recent
accomplishments, learn about
work underway now, and look at
the challenges ahead.
Andersen’s address will look
across city government at the
projects, priorities, and challenges
shaping the city’s work today.
As she approaches the end of her
term after nine years on the City
Council, she’ll also reflect on how
her perspective has changed after
seeing firsthand what it takes to
deliver the services, projects, and
programs residents rely on.
“After nine years on the City
Council, I have a deep apprecia-
tion for what it takes to make this
city work,” said Mayor Ander-
sen. “We have much to celebrate,
but we also have real challenges
in front of us. I hope people will
come spend the evening with us
and leave with a stronger sense of
where Piedmont stands today.”

ing – and stay for the conversa-

understand what the city is work-

and get a broader view of the

with Councilmembers, city
staff, and neighbors. Commu-

mont.ca.gov/SOTC-RSVP. All
are welcome, and sharing with

November 3 Election
On November 3, Piedmont
voters will elect representatives
to fill three seats on the Pied-

state, county, and special district
offices. The ballot also includes
a proposed increase to the City’s
Real Estate Transfer Tax and 14
statewide ballot measures.

County voters will receive a
vote-by-mail ballot. The Regis-

information guides on September
24 and will begin mailing ballots
starting Monday, October 5. Sign

already registered, check your

ber 19 to confirm that your infor-

disaster preparedness
The Piedmont Fire Depart-
ment is asking community
members to complete a brief
disaster preparedness survey
by October 30. The survey will
measure changes since 2024 and
help guide future preparedness
efforts.
Preparedness knowledge and
actions have changed since the
city’s first community survey in
2024. This survey will help the
city understand how prepared the
community is for earthquakes,
wildfires, and other disasters.
The survey should take about
5-7 minutes to complete and is
available at piedmont.ca.gov/
DisasterSurvey. The city’s 2024
survey showed that many respon-
dents recognized disaster risk but
had not taken some basic pre-
paredness steps.
Among respondents:
•
73% were registered for AC
Alert
•
22% had a current household
emergency communication
plan
•
34% had a current two-week
emergency water supply
•
27% felt confident or very
confident in their knowledge
of how to prepare for disasters
This year’s survey revisits
many of these measures and
includes new questions about how
the city’s preparedness efforts
have developed. This includes
earthquake safety and steps that
residents can take to minimize
wildfire risks at home.
The survey will ask where
people turn for information
during an emergency, what gets
in the way of becoming bet-
ter prepared, and what kinds of
resources would be most useful.
Since the 2024 survey, Pied-
mont Fire has expanded pre-
paredness outreach and commu-
nity engagement, including:
•
Updating Piedmont’s Local
Hazard Mitigation Plan with
extensive community partici-
pation
•
Increasing education about
wildfire home hardening and
defensible space, including a
series of presentations to com-
munity groups
•
Conducting a practical wild-
fire evacuation exercise in the
Blair/Scenic/Alta neighbor-
hood and creating an at-home
evacuation exercise available
to all households
•
Continuing year-round out-
reach on emergency alerts,
evacuation readiness, and
household preparedness
The survey data will help the
city evaluate where the work is
having an impact and what gaps
remain. It will also establish a
stronger baseline for earthquake
preparedness as Piedmont Fire
looks to expand outreach in this
area.
Results will help guide future
communications, educational
resources, exercises, and com-
munity programs. Complete the
survey by October 30 at pied-
mont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. For
resources and information about
preparing for disasters, visit pied-
mont.ca.gov/Disaster.

By Jake Lannon
At the September 22 City
Council meeting, the Coun-
cil voted to award the Moraga
Avenue Pedestrian Safety Proj-

for $785,533. The project will
install safety improvements as
recommended in the Piedmont
Safer Streets Plan. Construc-
tion is expected to begin in early
October along Moraga Avenue
between Ramona Avenue and
Red Rock Avenue.
The project will install bulb-
outs and high-visibility crosswalk
striping at the intersection of
Ramona and Moraga. The inter-
section of Monticello & Moraga
will receive a landscaped pedes-
trian refuge island and high-visi-
bility crosswalk striping. The last
intersection, Mesa & Moraga,
will receive a bulb-out, flash-
ing beacons, and a repositioned
crosswalk for improved visibility.
Interim Public Works Direc-
tor Rich Cunningham presented
the project to the City Council,
detailing some of the changes the
project will make.
“The intersection between
Moraga and Monticello, which
you have to walk 120 feet across
that intersection to cross it, was
not safe, and so we’ve put a traf-
fic island there. Part of that traffic
island is set aside for landscape,
and we’re bringing water across
the street from the cemetery
planted area via a pipe that will be
installed before paving the Mor-
aga Avenue section. The design
also includes preservation of the
bike lane,” said Cunningham.
The city will fund the proj-
ect through an Alameda County
Transportation Commission
(ACTC) grant, which awarded
the city $748,000 for design and
construction. The ACTC funds
transportation improvements
throughout Alameda County
that facilitate safe, efficient, and
accessible travel for all types of
transportation.
The City’s 2021 Safer Streets
Plan identified the Mesa/Moraga
intersection as the highest-prior-
ity location for citywide pedes-
trian safety enhancements, pri-
oritizing intersections based on
proximity to a school, location on
an arterial street, and inclusion on
a bike/bus route. Moraga Avenue
is one of the few arterial road-
ways within the City of Piedmont
eligible for regional transporta-
tion funding.
“There’s been almost uniform
support across the community. We
got a lot of nice emails, proactive
people up and down Moraga who
are all for it,” said Cunningham.
The contract agreement with
Terocons Inc. is for 16 weeks to
complete the work.

Barbara Lee announces $5,000,000 in state funding for Fairyland
By Jay Russell
On Monday, October 5,
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee
announced that Children’s Fairy-
land has secured a $5,000,000
allocation from the state of Cal-
ifornia to close out phase one of
its capital investment in the park.
The funds are designed to facil-
itate the initial stages of resto-
ration and revitalization.
“It’s really a storybook that
comes to life. Regardless of how
old you are or young you are, my
family can attest to the fact, this
is a dream come true,” said Lee.
Children’s Fairyland CEO
Kymberly Miller elucidated the
details of the funding, $3,000,000
will be designated to the park’s
capital investment to make “sure
we are taking care of this physical
space for 76 more years.”
The remaining two million
will go to the park’s general oper-
ations. The funds come from the
state’s budget which has allocated
$14 million for Oakland commu-
nity organizations, small busi-
nesses, public safety, and transi-
tional housing.
Other Oakland institutions
receiving state funding include:
Juntos Fruitvale Cultural Arts
Center, Samuel Merritt Univer-
sity’s human trafficking preven-
tion initiative, commercial cor-
ridors across Oakland, the city’s
Department of Violence Preven-
tion and The Holland transitional
housing facility.
“For 76 years, Fairyland has
given Oakland’s children a place
to imagine what’s possible. I
still remember bringing my sons
here, and today we’re making
sure the next generation gets
that same magic. This $5 million
is a proud victory for Oakland
because every dollar we put into
community spaces comes back
to us in the children they raise,”
said Lee.
Children’s Fairyland has been
a vital part of Oakland’s culture
since opening in 1950. As the
park that pioneered children’s
entertainment in this country,
Fairyland forever changed the
landscape of “family fun” as it is
known today. Children’s Fairy-
land is ten acres of green space
on the shores of Lake Merritt,
designed for outdoor play and
low-tech, high-touch hands-on
learning. It is a rare and increas-
ingly precious resource for chil-
dren.
The $5 million allocation will
fund numerous initiatives within
Fairyland’s strategic capital
investment plan, including
essential infrastructure and facil-
ity upgrades. Miller describes the
funding as foundational, rather
than final.
“This funding is a launchpad,
not a landing place. We have
much more work to do to create
the Fairyland of tomorrow. We’re
deeply grateful to Governor New-
som, Mayor Lee, and our State
of California partners for recog-
nizing what Fairyland means to
this community, to Oakland, and
to the entire Bay Area. We are
laying the groundwork for Fairy-
land’s financial sustainability so
we can continue to be a safe and
inclusive environment for play-

By Julia Stokes
On Wednesday, September
30, Piedmont High School held
its annual Consent Assembly
for seniors and freshmen. The
assembly, organized by act-
ing teacher Kim Taylor, junior
Stella Joseph, and senior Ben
Ramakrishnan, involved cur-
rent PHS students reading real
stories from anonymous PHS
graduates about their experi-
ences involving sexual assault
and consent.
“The purpose of the Consent
Assembly is to bring awareness
and educate people about how to
stay safe and how to prevent these
stories from happening again,”
junior Ida Marshall said.
Marshall was one of 16 stu-
dents who read stories. Although
Marshall is enrolled in acting,
students do not need to take act-
ing to present in the assembly. A
goal of the assembly is for peo-
ple from across the school to be
involved.
“I think it went well. All of the
other story readers were really
talented and I thought we made
the stories sound really real. I
heard stories about people being
affected by it,” Marshall said.
PHS also has a lunch club,
Piedmont for Consent (P4C), that
focuses on spreading awareness
about consent. According to P4C
co-president junior Sophia Puck-
ett, the club’s goal is to make sure
everyone feels comfortable about
consent and their personal bound-
aries.

this year include giving presen-
tations about what consent is at
elementary schools in Piedmont,

elective class at Piedmont Middle
School.

presentations for the elementary

ett said. “It’s an elective class,

ing awareness to this stuff is not

To take or not to take: that is the
PSAT and preACT question
By Ayla Blanford
After years of colleges mov-
ing away from requiring stan-
dardized testing, the admissions
process is shifting once again.
As more universities reinstate
SAT or ACT requirements, high
school students are reconsidering
the role tests, like the PSAT, play
in their college preparation.
During COVID-19, many uni-
versities stopped requiring test
scores as part of their application
process, shifting to test-optional
or test-blind. As testing gains
popularity, many students view
the PSAT as their first step of the
college application process.
“I took the PSAT to get a base-
line of what my score was with-
out studying, so that I could com-
pare it to my preACT score to see
which one I was better at,” junior
Chiara Silvio said.
Students often take these
exams in their sophomore year
of high school, so they can know
which test they want to take and
are most confident in junior year.
“I wanted to see which one I
was better at so junior year I can
really focus on studying,” sopho-
more Naomi Jerez said.
Although the PSAT has
become increasingly popular,
some students are choosing to
use other resources to determine
which direction they want to go
in.
“I did not take the PSAT; I
didn’t sign up for it because I plan
to take the online ones at home,”
junior Kyla Williams said. “I was
also going to take the SAT in
December, January, and another
one in March.”
As top schools switch to being
test-required, it affects students
differently depending on their
educational experiences and
future goals.
“A lot of people study for it,
and it’s not actually accurate, it’s
more about the tools you have
available to you than how well
you’d naturally do,” Silvio said.
While preparation plays a
large role in a student’s success
when taking a standardized test,
each student nationwide is taking
the same test. This uniformity
provides colleges with a base-
line to help determine a student’s
admission.
“Giving your grades or just
your transcript only shows in com-
parison to your school,” Williams
said. “For the SAT, it’s an overall
evaluation that doesn’t solely com-
pare to your surroundings.”
With the increase in resources
available to students, standard-
ized tests help colleges determine
how a student truly performs.
“Nowadays you can get good
grades by taking online classes,
and get into a good school,” Jerez
said. “With a standardized test,
everyone’s taking the same thing,
so it’s easier to compare scores
objectively.”
Taking the PSAT and preACT
is not a required step for the real
SAT or ACT, and can take mul-
tiple hours depending on testing
location. PreACT exams were
conducted in the PHS STEAM
building on Saturday, October 3,
starting at 8:45 a.m. and lasting
for two hours and 45 minutes.
“The test was really drain-
ing, and it was a lot harder than I
thought it was going to be,” Silvio
said.
However, many students say
the benefits outweigh the effort
required.
“I’ll be able to know which
format I like better and I’ll also
get an idea of the test taking envi-
ronment,” Jerez said.
Along with prepping students
for the SAT, taking the PSAT
offers students a series of other
benefits to support their college
applications.
“You can sign up for National
Merit, because it helps you qual-
ify if you take the PSAT,” Wil-
liams said.
For the class of 2026, many
universities have announced their
switch from test optional to test
required. Cornell University,
Yale University, Columbia Uni-
versity and Princeton Univer-
sity are some of many that have
announced their change. Many
schools have also announced
changes to their requirements that
won’t take effect for a few more
years. The University of Califor-
nia schools (UC Berkeley, UCSB,
UCLA, etc.) are still test-free for
the fall 2027 admission, and are
reviewing whether or not to bring
back testing for future applicants,
according to the University of
California.
Ayla Blanford is a junior at
Piedmont High School and a
student writer intern with the
Piedmont Post.

Bringing Harvest Festival scarecrows to life
By Jay Russell
Every year, Harvest Festival
scarecrows are constructed by
Piedmont students to be auc-
tioned off in Piedmont Park
during the event to fund the
schools. The Havens TK pump-
kin and 3rd-grade turkey scare-
crows both started as giant bal-
loons coated with several layers
of Piedmont Post paper strips and
wood glue before coming to life
at the festival.
Normally, each grade at the
three elementary school makes
its own scarecrow, but this year
some grades combined forces and
others did not participate. Those
that were on display were fantas-
tic. The Havens creators of two of
the seven scarecrows shared their
process with the Post.
“Due to drying time, we could
only apply a couple of layers per
day, working over several week-
ends alongside some late-night
prep work. My kids, Simone and
Sloane, did a lot of the initial
papier-mâché work before our
scheduled class work parties,”
said parent Holen Brady.

nicating with her other defensive

SF Playhouse presents Peter Pan Goes Wrong
By Allyson Aleksey
San Francisco Playhouse
is presenting Peter Pan Goes
Wrong, a comedy about an ama-
teur theater company attempting
to stage Peter Pan while a series
of mishaps threatens to derail the
production.
Written by Henry Lewis,
Henry Shields and Jonathan Sayer,
the play follows the fictional Corn-
ley Polytechnic Drama Society as
its members take on J.M. Barrie’s
classic story. The production fea-
tures flying rigs, sword fights and
a crocodile, along with forgotten
lines, malfunctioning scenery and
rivalries that spill onto the stage.
The play is by the creators
of The Play That Goes Wrong,
which similarly follows a fictional
theater troupe whose production
goes increasingly awry. Peter
Pan Goes Wrong premiered in
London in 2013 before later mov-
ing to the West End and Broad-
way.
Susi Damilano directs the
San Francisco production. The
cast includes Greg Ayers, Joe
Ayers, Maggie Mason, Christian
McCooey, Ezra Reaves, Renee
Rogoff, Patrick Russell, Sophie
Schulman, Terrance Austin
Smith, Jomar Tagatac and Phae-
dra Tillery-Boughton, among
others.

ning and matinee performances

ute intermission, and is recom-

with Escher String Quartet
Escher String Quartet
By Allyson Aleksey
Music at Kohl Mansion will
open its 44th season on October
18, with a performance by the
Escher String Quartet, an inter-
nationally recognized chamber
ensemble based in New York City.
The Escher String Quartet
features Adam Barnett-Hart
and Bryan Lee on violin, Pierre
Lapointe on viola and Brook
Speltz on cello. Formed in 2005
and named for Dutch graphic
artist M.C. Escher, the quartet
is known for performances com-
bining technical precision, inter-
pretive depth and a distinctive
ensemble sound.
The program will feature three
works from the string quartet
repertoire: Haydn’s Quartet in G
major, Op. 76, No. 1; Shostakov-
ich’s Quartet No. 3 in F major,
Op. 73; and Brahms’ Quartet in A
minor, Op. 51, No. 2.
The Escher String Quartet
serves as Artists of the Chamber
Music Society of Lincoln Center
and has performed at venues and
festivals including Wigmore Hall
in London, the Concertgebouw in
Amsterdam, the Kennedy Cen-
ter in Washington, D.C., and the
Auditorium du Louvre in Paris.
The ensemble has received
several honors, including an
Avery Fisher Career Grant and
Lincoln Center’s Martin E. Segal
Award. Its recording projects have
included the complete string quar-
tets of composers Alexander Zem-
linsky and Felix Mendelssohn.
The concert will begin at
7 p.m. at Kohl Mansion, 2750
Adeline Drive in Burlingame.
A pre-concert talk by Stanford
cellist and educator Christopher
Costanza will begin at 6 p.m., fol-
lowed by a complimentary glass
of wine and dessert after the per-
formance at 9 p.m.
Music at Kohl Mansion’s 2026-
27 season includes eight perfor-
mances through May 2, 2027, fea-
turing chamber music ensembles
and artists from the United States
and Europe. Performances take
place in the historic Kohl Man-
sion, also known as The Oaks,
which was built in 1914 and listed
on the National Register of His-
toric Places in 1982.
Tickets and season subscrip-
tions are available at www.musi-
catkohl.org.

What does it mean to find
your voice—and a place to
belong? The Piedmont East Bay

explore that question at its 2026
Benefit Concert & Auction,
“The Sound of Home,” at 6 p.m.

Marina. The evening will cele-
brate extraordinary young singers
and the community of families,
educators, alumni, volunteers,
accompanists, and supporters
who make their musical journey
possible.
Led by award-winning Artis-

received the 1st Prize Solo Com-
petition award at the Golden Gate
International Choral Festival. For

tion is about far more than learn-
ing to sing.
“Choral music is one of the
most powerful ways for young
people to build connections with
each other and the world around
them,” says Tuan. “Our singers
learn to listen to each other, to
share their voices in a way that
empowers the whole team, and
to explore different cultures and
perspectives through the univer-
sal language of music. As our
alumni remind us, those experi-
ences last for a lifetime.”

regardless of financial circum-
stances. Financial assistance is
central to the organization’s com-
mitment to building a community
where every singer belongs.

that mission while celebrating
the full circle of community sur-
rounding the choir.

community much bigger than
themselves,” says Tuan. “The
transformative experiences sing-
ers experience wouldn’t be pos-
sible without the alumni who
come back to teach and volun-
teer, the families who support
them through the program, and
the supporters who give so gen-
erously of their time, talent, and
treasure to ensure every singer
finds a home at PEBCC.”

phony Orchestra (YPSO), Cal-
ifornia’s oldest youth orchestra

landmark 90th Anniversary Sea-
son, celebrating nine decades of
guiding young musicians toward
excellence through orchestral
music, education, and commu-
nity. The 2026–27 anniversary
season will feature four concerts
spanning music from across cen-
turies and cultures.
Founded in Berkeley in 1936
by conductor Jessica Marcelli,
when women conductors were
exceedingly rare, YPSO enters
its 90th season following a suc-
cessful concert tour of Finland
and Sweden in June 2026. From
its Berkeley roots, the orches-
tra has grown to bring together
young musicians from across the
San Francisco Bay Area. Today,
under Music Director and Con-
ductor David Ramadanoff, YPSO
continues a tradition of challeng-
ing young musicians with great
orchestral repertoire while foster-
ing accomplishment, community,
and a lifelong passion for music.
“I’m very proud to be part of
an organization that has been pro-
viding young people the oppor-
tunity to play great music for
90 seasons,” Ramadanoff said.
“During my 38 years as Music
Director, it has been exciting and
heartwarming to help this orches-
tra develop into an outstanding
ensemble capable of playing the
wonderful and challenging music
we have programmed this sea-
son.”

concert on Saturday, November 7,
2026, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church
Berkeley. YPSO will open its

Festival Overture, Debussy’s
Nocturnes, and Brahms’ Sym-
phony No. 1.

place on Saturday, February 20,
2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church
Berkeley. The winter concert fea-
tures Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and
Juliet Fantasy-Overture, Gabri-
ela Lena Frank’s Three Latin
American Dances, and other
works, including music by Ralph
Vaughan Williams. The spring

WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Walking on Wednesday
Wednesday Walkers discover that
“Nace is Nice!”
By Ken Hubbert
Braving another warm day
on Sept. 30, the last day of the
month, 50 members of the Pied-
mont Recreation Department’s
Walking on Wednesdays group
and five of their canine com-
panions gathered at the Exedra
excited to see if Nace Avenue
really is nice.
Leading our walk and tour was
Pat Keller, a long-time Piedmont
resident and Wednesday walker.
Having lived on Nace Avenue for
years, Pat was well qualified to
relate the history of the area and
provide information about some
of the homes.
We began the walk heading in
the direction of Dracena Park. As
we walked through the park on
our way to Nace, Park Commis-
sioner Jack Fischrup noted that
there are now four great horned
owls in residence.
Nace is a tiny street with 27
houses. One unusual feature of
Nace is that it’s L-shaped, mak-
ing a 90-degree turn toward the
middle. The street was named
after Frank C. Havens’ secretary,
John Nace. At the time, it was
common to name streets after
the people who were involved in
developing the city. Nace is now a
popular street for young families,
with approximately 28 kids on it.
The first house we visited
was 22 Nace. It was built in
1906 for $2,820. We were fortu-
nate enough to encounter one of
the owners, KT, who graciously
invited us to come into her mag-
nificent backyard. It’s a breath-
taking and fun little surprise
when you enter the rear. The first
thing you notice is the immensity
of the outdoor living space with
beautiful views of Piedmont. In
addition there was a hot tub sur-
rounded by redwood decking,
a wooden, round-shaped sauna
with a cold plunge adjacent, and
an outdoor shower. To top things
off, an inviting outdoor cabana
with sofas tempted some of the
walkers to sit and relax.
Leaving 22 Nace, we walked
down the street to 42 Nace, which
has an uncommon flat roof. Pat
explained to the group that a fire
in the 1950s destroyed the origi-
nal pitched roof which was then
replaced by the flat roof.
Continuing just next door, we
visited 46 Nace, the present res-
idence of Dave and Kathy Yam.
Known as the “Gibson house,” it
was built in 1910 by the Fenton
family of ice cream fame. The
original house had lath and plas-
ter walls and the beams were first
generation old-growth redwood.
The Smith family moved
in around 1912 and the home
remained in the family until 1991
(79 years!). It is reported that they
planted the large Catalpa tree out
front, which is now a Piedmont
Heritage Tree. However, a neigh-
bor, Mrs. Gibson, claimed to have
grown up at 46 Nace and her
father planted the tree. Winnifred
inherited the house and married
Orrin Smith sometime between
1940 and 1950. They had no chil-
dren, but all of the family cele-
brations were held at the house.
Orrin was a wood shop teacher
at McClymonds High School in
Oakland and had a great work-
shop in the basement. The shelves
and drawers for storing hardware
were built by his students as a
shop project.
Orrin and Winnifred remod-
eled the house extensively both
inside and outside, excavating a
basement and using the surplus
soil to level the backyard. Next,
they dug out the front and built
a garage. In 1976, Winnifred
started the “Nace is Nice” block
party to celebrate the Fourth of
July. The current owner, Kathy,
inherited the block party tradition
and revived it in the 1990s.
When Winnifred passed away,
her sister Barbara became the
executor of the estate. Barbara
was the mother of one of Kathy
Yam’s best friends. At the time,
Kathy and her husband Dave
Route map
were looking for a home to buy
since their daughter Amy was
about to begin kindergarten.
Fortunately for Dave and Kathy,
Barbara agreed to sell the house
in time for Amy’s schooling.
Since moving in, Dave and
Kathy have extensively remod-
eled the house: adding a deck
to the back, building a second
story, re-shingling, constructing
interior stairs to the basement,
and assembling a new roof for
the garage. In 2021, the house
received the Design Award in
the Excellence in Architecturally
Consistent Design Category from
the City. The added garage was
the winner of the City’s Excel-
lence in Integrated Garage Design
in 2024. Dave provided the group
with ink-on-linen drawings of
the original house plans, as well
as two photo albums of the 1950
remodel.
Crossing the street to our final
stop, we ended our tour at 35
Nace, the home of Greg and Pat
Keller. Walkers were directed
into a lushly landscaped back-
yard. Beneath a slatted roof arbor,
a table of ice cold water, choco-
late chip cookies and chocolate
cake were waiting. Enough suste-
nance to fuel the walkers on their
uphill hike back to their Exedra
start.
All the walkers agreed, Nace
is really nice!!!
For further reading, “Queen of
the Hills: The Story of Piedmont,
A California City” by Evelyn
Craig Pattiani mentions on page
92 a Mabel Nace.

open to the public. Registration
with the Piedmont Recreation

The Wine Corner
Savoie: France’s Alpine wines
By Pierre DuMont
High in the French Alps,
where vineyards cling to steep
slopes beneath snow-capped
peaks, the wines of Savoie are
gaining attention for their distinc-
tive character and sense of place.
For generations, Savoie’s
vineyards have been closely tied
to the region’s mountain com-
munities. Today, a new genera-
tion of winemakers is bringing
renewed energy to an area once
known primarily to French locals
and Alpine holidaymakers. The
result is a collection of wines that
can be remarkably fresh, miner-
al-driven and unlike those pro-
duced in France’s better-known
regions.
White wines dominate Savoie’s
production, with the Jacquère
grape playing a central role.
Light-bodied and crisp, Jacquère
produces wines with lively acidity
and subtle floral and citrus notes,
making them natural companions
to local mountain cuisine. Altesse,
another important white grape,
produces the more structured
and aromatic wines known as
Roussette de Savoie. My favorite
wine is Chignin-Bergeron, which
is made from the Rhone Valley’s
Roussanne grape.
The region also has its own red
specialties. Mondeuse, a tradi-
tional local grape, creates deeply
colored wines with bright acidity,
peppery spice and dark-fruit fla-
vors. Gamay and Pinot Noir are
also planted, adding further vari-
ety to the region’s offerings.
Savoie’s geography is central
to its identity. Vineyards are scat-
tered across valleys and foothills,
often at considerable elevations.
The cool Alpine climate allows
grapes to ripen slowly while
retaining the acidity that gives
the wines their characteristic
freshness.
That freshness is particularly
well suited to Savoie’s traditional
foods: fondue, raclette, tartiflette
and other rich mountain dishes.
The wines cut through the rich-
ness of the cheese and potatoes,
creating a pairing that reflects the
region itself.
As interest in distinctive, ter-
roir-driven wines continues to
grow, Savoie is increasingly find-
ing a place on the international
wine map. Its bottles offer some-
thing increasingly sought after
by modern wine drinkers: wines
with a strong sense of origin, tra-
dition and landscape.
Philippe Viallet:
a family name in
Savoie wine
At the foot of Mont Granier
in France’s Alpine Savoie region,
the name Philippe Viallet has
become closely associated with
the area’s distinctive wines. The
family wine story began in 1966,
when Marcel and Yvonne Vial-
let acquired a small vineyard in
Apremont. Their sons, Pierre and
Philippe, later continued the fam-
ily business, with Philippe help-
ing to develop it into both a wine
producer and wine merchant.
The Viallet range reflects
the diversity of Savoie’s moun-
tain vineyards. Among its best-
known wines is Apremont,
made from the Jacquère grape.
It is a light, crisp and refreshing
white wine with bright acidity.
Another important wine is Chi-
gnin-Bergeron, made from the
Roussanne grape and generally
fuller and more aromatic, with
flavors of ripe fruit and flowers.
Roussette de Savoie, made
from the Altesse grape, offers
another distinctive style, while
the winery’s red wines include
Mondeuse, one of Savoie’s tradi-
tional varieties, as well as Pinot
Noir and Gamay.
The winery also produces
Crémant de Savoie, a sparkling
wine, along with rosé wines.
Philippe Viallet’s wines offer
a taste of the Alpine landscape.
Fresh, lively and closely con-
nected to local grape varieties,
they demonstrate why Savoie is
attracting growing interest from
wine drinkers looking for wines
with a strong sense of place and a
character of their own.

Why AKC dog sports
are slowly dying
Coral the Great Dane poses for the judge, her handler hoping for a win
after paying high entry fees.
By Sierra Berrick
The world of competitive dog
sports can be one of the most
exciting for canine enthusiasts.
There is the opportunity to meet
fellow dog lovers, win awards
for your pup, and spend quality
time with them. Unfortunately,
fewer and fewer new people are
joining. Let’s examine a couple of
reasons that may explain this, and
hopefully drive current profes-
sionals in the American Kennel
Club (AKC) world to make some
changes.
Not everything is the fault of
individuals, but of our infrastruc-
ture. Simply put, money is an
issue. With the costs of operating
training clubs and events going
up just like the cost of living,
many people are being priced out
of dog shows. To enter a dog in
AKC conformation, the major-
ity of shows cost around $37 a
day. To compete in a four-day
show, that’s well over $100, not
counting the cost of travel and
food. Even newer sports, such
as Fast CAT, demonstrate signif-
icant costs on their entry forms.
In California, pre-entry for Fast
CAT, which allows two runs per
dog per day, costs between $28
and $35 per run. Considering this
sport is entirely based on partic-
ipation, the unfortunate truth is
that people are now paying for
their titles rather than needing to
demonstrate excellence with their
dog. For young people who may
have bachelor’s-degree-level jobs,
these prohibitively high entry
fees make it impossible for them
to get their foot in the door.
Lack of new exhibitors is a
big concern, not just because
it means dog shows are slowly
becoming an event only for the
wealthy, but because fewer com-
petitors means fewer champion-
ship points and majors. The AKC
point system is based on winning
against a certain number of dogs,
and with more competitors aging
out than entering the sport, it will
become markedly harder for indi-
viduals to achieve championship
titles with their dogs.
Now let’s talk about attitude.
Many people coming from pet
backgrounds assume that all dog
people are enthusiastic and kind.
Unfortunately, this is not always
so within the dog show world.
Many new participants at dog
shows report feeling unwelcome
and unsupported. Although there
is no clear reason for this, the idea
of people simply being competi-
tive does not fully explain it.
The high costs of entry, plus
feeling excluded by veterans
in the sport, unfortunately lead
many new exhibitors to quit
before they’ve really started. This
means that it is up to the old-tim-
ers in dog sports to open their
hearts to new competitors, and for
new competitors to set the tone
in the sport as welcoming going
forward. Perhaps the American
Kennel Club should consider the
long-term results of pricing out
exhibitors with these high entry
fees. Only time will tell if dog
enthusiasts are able to commit to
these necessary changes.

in service dog work, obedience,

The History of Piedmont
Guests, visitors and staff lined up in front of the Piedmont Springs Hotel for this undated photo, possibly the
grand opening in 1871.
Piedmont Springs Hotel, circa 1871
By Gail G. Lombardi
Part 2 in a series
It all started with the water.
It smelled awful, but it made his
old joints feel better. In the mid-
1850s, old Isaac Holmes dragged
a bathtub down the ravine to the
mineral springs on the side of
the hill. Soaking in the mineral
water helped to ease his rheuma-
tism. When he died, the mineral
springs were forgotten.
In the 1860s, these mineral
springs (said to contain sul-
phur, magnesia, iodine and iron)
were re-discovered in the ravine
behind today’s Exedra, the cur-
rent location of Bushy Dell Creek.
Drinking or soaking in mineral
water was believed to have great
curative powers. These mineral
springs were similar to the pop-
ular mineral waters in Calistoga,
and they were only three miles
from downtown Oakland.
Investors quickly saw an
opportunity to develop the
springs and build a hotel to
accommodate visitors who
came to “take the waters.” They
selected the name “Piedmont,”
meaning “foot of the hills,” thus
securing the name of Piedmont
to our locale. The investors
formed the Piedmont Land Com-
pany to buy 350 acres around the
ravine, build the hotel and sell
any adjoining land not needed
for the hotel purposes as resi-
dential lots.
In 1871, the Piedmont Springs
Hotel opened near today’s Exedra
as a first-class resort. The photo
of the hotel shows only the north-
ern portion of the building, which
had two wings and was twice the
size of the building as shown.
The hotel had a wide veranda,
20 first-class bedrooms and
two suites, five dining rooms,
telegraph service, and a Grand
Saloon (for men only) with an ele-
gant mahogany bar, billiard table,
spittoons and a pot-bellied stove.
The ladies’ entrance allowed
women to enter the hotel, avoid
the saloon and proceed directly
to the main dining room with its
crystal chandelier, linen table-
cloths and fine china.
The hotel quickly became a
popular destination and drew
visitors who passed a pleasant
Sunday at Piedmont Springs,
strolling the meandering paths
to the mineral springs and enjoy-
ing an excellent lunch or dinner.
The dining rooms served fresh
meat from nearby ranches, milk
and butter from Blair’s Dairy,
A map shows the location of Piedmont Springs Hotel and Sulphur
Springs at the end of Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) in 1883.
and fresh fruit and vegetables
from its gardens. The hotel also
offered fine wine and liquor for
those who did not care for min-
eral water. Fashionable San Fran-
ciscans would come for a week
to escape the summer fog. Many
hotel guests enjoyed the mild
weather and views of San Fran-
cisco Bay and decided to buy land
and build their homes here.
The hotel thrived until 1892,
when a spark from a faulty chim-
ney started a fire on the roof.
Hotel guests watched helplessly
as the hotel burned to the ground
before firefighters could arrive
from downtown Oakland. The
site would not be empty for long...
but that’s another story.
The mineral springs are still
in Piedmont Park, but they were
capped in the 1950s because the
sulphur fumes offended many
residents. The historical marker
at the Veterans’ Building gives
the location of the springs.
To learn more about Pied-
mont’s history, see the Piedmont
Historical Society website: Pied-
monthistorical.org.

Nancy Beninati
(NancyforPiedmont.com)
I support and appreciate the
hard work of our police, fire,
and city employees. I believe all
Piedmont employees should be
paid fairly and competitively,
consistent with what the City can
responsibly afford.
The City must carefully eval-
uate any proposals and the long-
term fiscal impacts to make a
decision that best serves our com-
munity as a whole. While Pied-
mont has some wealthy residents,
the City’s revenue streams are lim-
ited and rely heavily on property
taxes. Any significant increase in
compensation or benefits must be
considered in the context of the
entire City budget, the needs of all
City employees, and other import-
ant City priorities.
I support Measure GG
because it would provide the City
with additional ongoing revenue
for parks, recreation, infrastruc-
ture, maintenance, and other City
needs, including employee com-
pensation. But additional revenue
does not eliminate the need to
make difficult budget choices.
As a councilmember, I would
support fair compensation while
also making sure that any agree-
ment is financially sustainable
and treats all of our employees
fairly. Ultimately, the Council
and City will have to balance
competitive compensation with
the City’s overall financial con-
straints and the priorities of the
community.
Adam Hundt
(AdamHundt.com)
The City Council should pres-
ent to the community a compre-
hensive plan for the police and
fire departments. We need to
maintain these services for the

aries are 136% of the amount

ics), or something else? I believe

opers to build below-market-rate

One of the main benefits of

ber one priority; our property can
